nameStory: This fungal disease gets its name from the golden-orange coloration of its fruiting bodies that emerge from infected dogwood bark. The word 'canker' comes from the Latin 'cancer,' meaning crab, because these diseases spread outward like crab legs, creating sunken, dead areas that girdle and kill branches.
description: Dogwood golden canker is a fungal disease that attacks flowering dogwoods and other dogwood species throughout New England. It appears as sunken, discolored patches of bark that eventually girdle branches and kill them. The disease produces tiny, bright orange to golden fruiting bodies that peek through the dead bark like miniature volcanoes. Small infections may only affect individual branches, but severe cases can kill entire trees.

idTips.label: Golden fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for bright orange to golden-yellow, pinhead-sized bumps pushing through dead bark - they feel slightly raised and gritty when touched gently

idTips.label: Sunken cankers
idTips.description: Infected bark areas appear depressed below the healthy bark surface, often with a darker, reddish-brown discoloration around the edges

idTips.label: Branch dieback
idTips.description: Affected branches show wilting leaves that turn brown but often remain attached, creating a flagging effect visible from a distance

idTips.label: Bark cracking
idTips.description: Dead bark around cankers often splits and peels away in strips, revealing darker wood underneath that may feel slightly soft or spongy

idTips.label: Host specificity
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on dogwood trees, particularly flowering dogwood with its distinctive opposite leaves and layered branching pattern

habitat: Found throughout New England's forests, parks, and residential areas wherever dogwood trees grow, particularly in understory positions and forest edges. Most common in mixed hardwood forests with well-drained soils and partial shade. Urban and suburban plantings of flowering dogwood are especially susceptible, particularly trees stressed by drought, poor soil, or mechanical damage.

seasonality.spring: Early infections may show as slightly sunken bark areas, often overlooked until later symptoms develop. New spores are released during wet spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Cankers expand rapidly in hot, humid weather, and the characteristic golden fruiting bodies become most visible. Branch dieback and leaf wilting are most apparent.
seasonality.fall: Dead leaves often remain attached to killed branches, creating obvious brown flags against healthy foliage. Bark splitting becomes more pronounced.
seasonality.winter: Orange fruiting bodies remain visible on bare branches, making this an excellent time for identification. Canker damage is most apparent without leaf cover.

funFact: This fungus can actually survive in dead dogwood wood for years, slowly releasing spores every time it rains - meaning that decorative dogwood branches brought indoors can continue spreading the disease to healthy trees outside for seasons after they're cut!
confusionNotes: Often confused with other canker diseases or mechanical damage to dogwood bark, but the distinctive golden-orange fruiting bodies are diagnostic. Remember: 'Golden bumps mean dogwood dumps' - if you see those bright orange spots, the branch is likely doomed.
contextualKnowledge: This disease has become increasingly problematic as flowering dogwoods face multiple stressors including drought, soil compaction, and another serious disease called dogwood anthracnose. Many arborists now recommend native alternatives like pagoda dogwood or kousa dogwood for new plantings.
compareHints: As the only Aurantioporthe species commonly found in New England, it's most easily confused with other canker-causing fungi in the family Cryphonectriaceae. However, the bright golden-orange color of its fruiting bodies is distinctive - most related canker fungi produce darker brown or black fruiting structures. The combination of dogwood host specificity and golden coloration makes identification relatively straightforward.
